opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core challenge is that the physical world is incredibly unforgiving and incredibly diverse at the same time. With language models, you had the entire internet as a training corpus: trillions of tokens of text that people had already produced. Robotics doesn't have that. There's no giant pre-existing dataset of robots folding laundry, opening every kind of drawer, or handling a slippery glass. So the first problem is simply data. How do you get enough rich, varied experience of physical interaction to learn from?

The way I think about it, there are a few complementary paths. One is simulation. You can run millions of episodes in a physics engine, randomize lighting, textures, friction and object shapes, and get a policy that's robust enough to transfer to the real world. But simulation is always an approximation. Contact dynamics, deformable objects and things like cloth or liquids are still really hard to model faithfully, so you hit a sim-to-real gap.

The second path is real-world data collection, through teleoperation, human demonstrations, or fleets of robots gathering experience as they work. That's expensive and slow, but it's grounded in reality. More and more, I think the winning approach combines the two: use simulation and large-scale video of humans doing things to build broad priors about how the world works, then fine-tune with targeted real-world data.

The third piece is the shift toward foundation models for robotics. Instead of training a narrow policy for one task in one environment, you train a large model on diverse data across many tasks and embodiments, so it develops something like common sense about physics: objects fall, things can be pushed or grasped, doors swing on hinges. Vision-language models help a lot here, because they bring semantic understanding. The robot knows what a mug is and what "put it away" probably means, and the action layer has to translate that into precise motor control.

Underneath all of this is the problem of generalization and reliability. A demo that works 80% of the time is impressive in a lab, but in a warehouse, a home or a hospital you need something like 99.9%, and you need the robot to fail safely when it doesn't know what to do. So for me the challenge isn't just teaching robots skills. It's teaching them to handle the long tail: the weird lighting, the unexpected object, the person walking by. That long tail is where most of the real work is right now.

r001.rationale: It contrasts the internet’s vast text corpus for language models with the lack of a large existing dataset of robots performing physical tasks.

r002.rationale: It says simulation is an approximation and explicitly identifies a sim-to-real gap that makes transfer difficult.

r003.rationale: It describes simulation, video, and real-world collection through teleoperation or demonstrations as complementary sources, then says to combine them and fine-tune with real-world data.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the fundamental problem is that the physical world doesn't come with labels. When you train a language model, you have the entire internet as a corpus of human thought already written down. When you train a vision model, you have billions of images with captions. Robots don't have that. There's no internet of robot experience sitting out there waiting to be scraped.

So the first challenge is just data. Every time a robot picks something up, that's a data point you had to generate yourself, in a real environment, with real hardware that breaks and drifts and behaves slightly differently from one unit to the next. That makes the data expensive and slow to collect compared to what we're used to in other parts of AI.

The second challenge is that physics is unforgiving in a way that text isn't. If a language model gets a word wrong, nobody gets hurt. If a robot misjudges the friction on a glass by a few percent, the glass is on the floor. The model has to reason about contact, force, weight, deformation, things that are hard to see and even harder to simulate perfectly. Simulation gets you a long way, and we lean on it heavily, but there's always a gap between the simulator and reality, and closing that gap is a big part of the job.

The third piece, and the one I find most interesting, is generalization. It's not that hard anymore to get a robot to do one task in one lab really well. What's hard is a robot that walks into a kitchen it's never seen, with objects it's never handled, and figures out what to do. That requires a kind of common-sense understanding of the world, how objects behave, what things are for, that humans pick up as toddlers by just bumping around and knocking things over.

What's changed in the last few years is that the big foundation models actually give us a shortcut to some of that common sense. They know what a mug is, they know you pour into the open end, they know a knife is sharp. The question we're working on is how to connect that semantic knowledge to the low-level control, the actual motor commands, so the robot can go from understanding the world in words to acting in it with its hands. That bridge, between knowing and doing, is really where the frontier is right now.

r001.rationale: It contrasts language models’ access to the internet as a corpus with robots’ lack of readily available physical-interaction data.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says there is a gap between simulation and reality that must be closed.

r003.rationale: It discusses simulation and real-world data, but does not identify teleoperation and video as ingredients combined in different proportions.

astra-6.text:
I think the challenge is that understanding the physical world and acting in it are really two different problems. A robot might recognize a cup, but that doesn’t mean it knows how firmly to grip it, whether it’s full, or what happens if it slips. Those are things people handle almost without thinking.

So you need a learning process that connects perception to action and then to feedback. The robot does something, observes what actually happened, and adjusts. Simulation can help you practice, but ultimately you have to deal with the variability of the real world—different surfaces, different lighting, people moving unpredictably.

The way I’d approach it is to start with a bounded task and make the robot reliable at that task, including recognizing when it’s uncertain and should stop. Then expand its capabilities. A successful demonstration is one thing; doing useful work consistently in an environment you don’t completely control is the real challenge.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare internet language data with scarce physical-interaction data for robots.

r002.rationale: It mentions simulation and real-world variability, but does not clearly identify a sim-to-real transfer gap as a training difficulty.

r003.rationale: The response mentions simulation but does not describe combining it with teleoperation and video as training ingredients.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the challenge is that understanding the physical world and being able to act in it are two different things. A robot might recognize a cup, but picking it up means understanding where it is, how to approach it, how much force to apply, and what to do if it moves or starts to slip.

And the real world is full of variation. The lighting changes, somebody puts something in the way, an object isn’t exactly where it was yesterday. You need a system that can respond to what’s actually happening, rather than just repeat a sequence that worked in a controlled setting.

So I think you start with a useful, well-defined task and build a feedback loop around it. Let the robot act, observe the result, and use that experience to improve. The goal is reliable behavior in the environment where the robot is going to work. That’s a much higher bar than getting a compelling demonstration once.

r001.rationale: The response discusses physical-world interaction but does not compare the abundance of internet language data with the scarcity of robot interaction data.

r002.rationale: It contrasts controlled settings with real-world variation, but does not identify simulation-to-reality transfer as a training difficulty.

r003.rationale: It recommends a feedback loop of acting, observing, and improving, but does not mention simulation, teleoperation, or video as combined training ingredients.
